notes.definition: Electromagnetism is the magnetic effect of an electric current: when a current flows through a wire, a magnetic field is produced around the wire. A solenoid with an iron core is an electromagnet.
explanation: When a current flows through a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced around the wire. This can be demonstrated by placing a plotting compass next to a wire connected to a power supply: when the current is switched on the needle turns, and when the current is reversed the needle points the opposite way. Iron filings sprinkled on a card around a vertical current-carrying wire form circles around the wire.

The magnetic field around a straight wire is a set of concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes at right angles to the wire. The direction of the field depends on the direction of the current and can be found with the right-hand grip rule: grip the wire with your right hand with your thumb pointing in the direction of the current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the field. Reversing the current reverses the field.

The strength of the magnetic field depends on the current through the wire and the distance from the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field. The field is strongest close to the wire and gets weaker further away, which is why the circles on a field diagram are drawn further apart as the distance from the wire increases.

Shaping a wire to form a coil called a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field, because the fields from each turn add together. The magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform: the field lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced. Outside the solenoid, the field has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. Using more turns or a larger current makes the field stronger.

Adding an iron core inside a solenoid greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field, because the iron becomes an induced magnet. A solenoid with an iron core is called an electromagnet. Its key advantage is that it can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed by changing the current. When the current is switched off, the soft iron core loses its magnetism quickly.
keyFacts: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around the wire.
The field around a straight wire is concentric circles centred on the wire.
Field direction depends on current direction (right-hand grip rule); reversing the current reverses the field.
Field strength increases with current and decreases with distance from the wire.
A solenoid is a coil of wire; coiling the wire makes the field stronger.
Inside a solenoid the field is strong and uniform.
Outside a solenoid the field is like that of a bar magnet.
An iron core inside a solenoid increases the field strength.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core; it can be switched on and off.
A compass placed near a current-carrying wire deflects, demonstrating the magnetic effect of a current.

keyTerms.definition: The production of a magnetic field by an electric current.
A long coil of wire; when a current flows it produces a strong, uniform field inside it.
A solenoid with an iron core, which gives a strong magnetic field that can be switched on and off.
A magnetic field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.
Grip the wire with the right thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field.
A piece of soft iron placed inside a coil; it becomes an induced magnet and strengthens the field.

workedExamples.title: Direction of the field around a wire
workedExamples.question: A vertical wire carries a current upwards. Viewed from above, is the magnetic field clockwise or anticlockwise?
steps: Use the right-hand grip rule: point your right thumb upwards (the current direction).
Your fingers curl anticlockwise when viewed from above.

workedExamples.title: Making an electromagnet stronger
workedExamples.question: State three ways of increasing the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid.
steps: The field comes from the current, so a larger current gives a stronger field.
Each turn adds its field, so more turns of wire give a stronger field.
An iron core becomes an induced magnet and adds to the field.
workedExamples.answer: Increase the current, increase the number of turns, add an iron core.

workedExamples.title: Finding the poles of a solenoid
workedExamples.question: Looking at one end of a solenoid, the current flows anticlockwise. Which pole is this end?
steps: Use the right-hand grip rule: curl your right fingers in the direction of the current (anticlockwise).
Your thumb points towards you, out of that end of the coil, which is the direction of the field inside.
Field lines leave a north pole, so this end is the north pole.
workedExamples.answer: This end is a north pole.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the field around a straight wire runs along the wire, parallel to the current.
misconceptions.right: In fact the field lines are circles around the wire, at right angles to the current.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the field around a wire has the same strength everywhere.
misconceptions.right: In fact the field is strongest close to the wire and weakens with distance, and it is stronger for a larger current.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the iron core of an electromagnet produces the magnetic field on its own.
misconceptions.right: In fact the current produces the field; the soft iron core becomes an induced magnet and makes the field much stronger, and it loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the field inside a solenoid is weakest because it is surrounded by wire.
misconceptions.right: In fact the field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform, because the fields from all the turns add together there.

realWorld: Scrapyard cranes use large electromagnets to lift steel cars and drop them by switching the current off.
Electric door locks, doorbells and relays use electromagnets that can be switched on and off.
MRI scanners in hospitals use very strong electromagnets (made from coils of wire) to produce detailed images of the body.
Circuit breakers use an electromagnet that pulls a switch open when the current becomes too large.
separateOnlyContent: Separate Physics students should be able to interpret diagrams of electromagnetic devices in order to explain how they work.

Relay: a small current in one circuit flows through an electromagnet, which attracts an iron armature and closes switch contacts in a second circuit. This lets a small, safe current switch on a large current (for example the starter motor in a car).

Electric bell: closing the switch magnetises the electromagnet, which attracts the iron armature so the hammer hits the gong; this breaks the circuit at the contact screw, the electromagnet switches off, the springy strip pulls the armature back, the circuit is completed again and the cycle repeats.

Circuit breaker: if the current becomes too large, the electromagnet becomes strong enough to pull an iron catch, which opens the switch and breaks the circuit. It can be reset once the fault is fixed.
examTips: When drawing the field around a straight wire, draw circles centred on the wire, getting further apart with distance, with arrows all going the same way round.
State the two factors for the strength of the field around a wire: the size of the current and the distance from the wire.
Describe the field inside a solenoid as 'strong and uniform' and outside as 'like a bar magnet'. These exact phrases score marks.
For a device diagram (separate Physics), explain in sequence: current flows, the iron core is magnetised, it attracts the iron armature, which causes the next event.
summary: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field.
Around a straight wire the field is concentric circles; direction set by the current.
The field is stronger for a larger current and closer to the wire.
A solenoid gives a strong, uniform field inside and a bar-magnet field outside.
An iron core makes an electromagnet much stronger.
Electromagnets can be switched on and off and their strength can be varied.

questions.question: What is produced around a wire when an electric current flows through it?
markScheme: 1 mark: A magnetic field
questions.explanation: A current always produces a magnetic field around the wire. This is the magnetic effect of a current.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a long straight wire passing vertically through a horizontal card. There is a current in the wire.
What shape are the magnetic field lines around the wire?

options: Concentric circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Lines from one end of the wire to the other
markScheme: 1 mark: Concentric circles centred on the wire
questions.explanation: The field lines form circles around the wire, in planes at right angles to it.

questions.question: What is an electromagnet?
options: A permanent magnet made of steel
A battery connected to a bulb
A solenoid with an iron core
markScheme: 1 mark: A solenoid with an iron core
questions.explanation: An electromagnet is a coil of wire (solenoid) with an iron core, which produces a strong field when current flows.

questions.question: Which change would make the magnetic field around a wire stronger?
options: Using a longer wire with the same current
markScheme: 1 mark: Increasing the current
questions.explanation: Field strength depends on the current: a larger current gives a stronger field. Reversing the current only changes the direction.

questions.question: What is the magnetic field like inside a long solenoid carrying a current?
options: Strongest at the centre of each wire only
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong and uniform
questions.explanation: Inside a solenoid the fields of all the turns add together, giving a strong, uniform field (straight, parallel lines).

questions.question: What does the magnetic field outside a solenoid look like?
options: Like the field of a bar magnet
markScheme: 1 mark: Like the field of a bar magnet
questions.explanation: Outside, a solenoid's field has the same shape as a bar magnet's field, with N and S poles at the ends.

questions.question: Why is soft iron used as the core of an electromagnet in a scrapyard crane?
options: It is a good electrical conductor
It is magnetised easily and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off
markScheme: 1 mark: It is magnetised easily and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off
questions.explanation: Soft iron strengthens the field while the current flows but loses its magnetism when switched off, so the crane can drop the load.

questions.question: A plotting compass is placed next to a wire. What happens to the needle when the current is reversed?
options: It points in the opposite direction
markScheme: 1 mark: It points in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the magnetic field, so the compass needle turns to point the opposite way.

questions.question:
A vertical wire carries a current downwards.
Figure 1 shows the wire viewed from above. The cross shows that the current is flowing into the page.
What is the direction of the magnetic field around the wire, viewed from above?

markScheme: 1 mark: Clockwise
questions.explanation: Right-hand grip rule: thumb pointing down; viewed from above, the fingers curl clockwise.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows one end of a solenoid. Viewed from this end, the current flows clockwise.
Which magnetic pole is this end of the solenoid?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif"><circle cx="210" cy="80" r="55" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="210" cy="80" r="40" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><polygon points="237.5,32.4 230.7,22.1 225.2,31.7" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="182.5,127.6 189.3,137.9 194.8,128.3" fill="currentColor"/><text x="210" y="170" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">The arrows show the direction of the current.</text></svg>

options: There is no pole at the end
markScheme: 1 mark: South
questions.explanation: Curl your right-hand fingers clockwise (as seen from that end): the thumb points away from you into the solenoid, so the field enters at this end. Field lines enter a south pole.

questions.question: At which point is the magnetic field of a long straight current-carrying wire weakest?
markScheme: 1 mark: 10 cm from the wire
questions.explanation: The field gets weaker with distance from the wire, so it is weakest at the greatest distance, 10 cm.

questions.question: Describe how you could show that there is a magnetic field around a wire carrying a current.
markScheme: 1 mark: place a plotting compass near the wire (or sprinkle iron filings on a card around the wire)
1 mark: the needle deflects (or the filings form circles) when the current is switched on
questions.explanation: The compass needle responds to the magnetic field produced by the current; with no current it points north.

questions.question: State two factors that affect the strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire.
markScheme: 1 mark: the size of the current
1 mark: the distance from the wire
questions.explanation: A bigger current gives a stronger field; the field weakens further from the wire.

questions.question: State three ways of increasing the strength of an electromagnet.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase the current
1 mark: increase the number of turns (coils)
1 mark: add (or use) an iron core
questions.explanation: Each of these increases the total magnetic field produced by the coil.

questions.question: Explain why an electromagnet is more useful than a permanent magnet for lifting and moving scrap steel.
markScheme: 1 mark: an electromagnet can be switched on and off
1 mark: so the steel can be released (dropped) where it is needed (or its strength can be varied)
questions.explanation: A permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so it would be very hard to release the steel.

questions.question: Explain why adding an iron core to a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field.
markScheme: 1 mark: the iron core becomes magnetised (an induced magnet) in the field of the coil
1 mark: its field adds to the field of the coil
questions.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material, so the solenoid's field induces magnetism in it, greatly strengthening the overall field.

questions.question: Describe the shape of the magnetic field inside and outside a solenoid.
markScheme: 1 mark: inside: strong and uniform (straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines)
1 mark: outside: similar to the field of a bar magnet
questions.explanation: These two phrases summarise the solenoid field pattern.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a horizontal card viewed from above. A vertical wire passes through the card. The current in the wire flows upwards, out of the card.
A plotting compass is placed on the card directly to the east of the wire.
Ignore the Earth's magnetic field.
State which way the compass needle points.
Explain how you know.

questions.explanation: Thumb up, fingers curl anticlockwise from above. Moving anticlockwise, a point to the east of the centre moves north.

questions.question: Explain why the magnetic field inside a solenoid is much stronger than the field around a single straight wire carrying the same current.
markScheme: 1 mark: the magnetic fields from each turn of the coil point in the same direction inside the solenoid
1 mark: so the fields add together (combine) to give a stronger field
questions.explanation: Coiling the wire lines up the fields of all the turns inside the coil, so they reinforce each other.

questions.question: Give one use of an electromagnet.
markScheme: 1 mark: any valid use, such as scrapyard crane, relay, electric bell, door lock, circuit breaker, MRI scanner, loudspeaker
questions.explanation: Electromagnets are used wherever a magnetic field must be switched or controlled.

questions.question: Describe the magnetic field pattern around a long straight wire carrying a current. Include how the pattern changes if the current is increased or reversed.
markScheme: Indicative content: concentric circles centred on the wire; in planes perpendicular to the wire; direction given by the right-hand grip rule; circles further apart further from the wire because the field is weaker; increasing the current makes the field stronger (lines closer together at each distance); reversing the current reverses the field direction (arrows reverse) but not the shape.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes shape and direction or strength variation and both changes correctly.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic description such as circles around the wire.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Shape (circles), variation with distance, and effects of current size and direction are the key ideas.

questions.question: What is a solenoid?
markScheme: 1 mark: A coil of wire
questions.explanation: A solenoid is a long coil of wire. With a current, it produces a magnetic field like a bar magnet.

questions.question:
Two long straight wires each carry a current.
Table 1 shows the current in each wire.
At which point is the magnetic field strongest?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 cm from wire Y
questions.explanation: Field strength increases with current and decreases with distance, so the strongest field is close to the wire with the larger current.
